rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as the position, which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.

The answer explicitly states that the technical documentation must include 'a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run', citing Annex IV point 1(e), which conveys the substance of the requirement.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No, the AI system is not "medium risk," because Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 has no such category and the device's MDR risk class does not transfer to it; the AI system is high-risk. Classification runs through the Annex I product route in Article 6(1), which is satisfied where both conditions are cumulatively met: under point (a), the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 appear at Annex I, point 11; and under point (b), that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market. Both limbs are fulfilled here, and Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market independently of the device. Because the route is Annex I and not Article 6(2), neither the Annex III use-case list nor the Article 6(3) derogation is available. Consequently the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements apply (Article 8), and under Article 43(3) the provider follows the MDR notified-body procedure, into which the AI Act requirements are integrated, with Annex VII points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of 4.6 also applying.
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: Answer correctly states that the AI Act has no 'medium-risk' category and explicitly identifies the AI system as high-risk.
Answer states that the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, specifically citing Regulation (EU) 2017/745 for medical devices.
Answer confirms that the product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment with reference to its placing on the market.
Answer explains that both conditions under Article 6(1) are cumulative and applies them regardless of the device's sectoral risk classification.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear regulatory prose without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, the system is not prohibited, and on that description it is not high-risk. Article 5(1) prohibits no one-to-one biometric verification practice; it reaches biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes under point (g) and real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement under point (h), neither of which this is. Annex III, point 1(a) expressly excludes AI systems intended for biometric verification whose sole purpose is confirming that a specific natural person is who he or she claims to be, so the Article 6(2) route is not triggered, absent another Annex III use case or an Annex I product route.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer states the system is not prohibited, correctly distinguishing it from prohibited practices under Article 5(1)(g) and (h).
The answer explicitly states the system is not high-risk, explaining that the Annex III trigger does not apply due to the exclusion.
The answer cites the exclusion in Annex III.1(a) for biometric verification systems with the sole purpose of confirming identity, matching the factual description given.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents regulatory reasoning in a deployable form.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 governs human oversight. It requires that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so they can be effectively overseen by natural persons while in use (Article 14(1)), with oversight measures commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, built into the system by the provider or identified for implementation by the deployer (Article 14(3)).
criteria_text: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that Article 14 governs human oversight.
The answer cites Article 14(1), which requires design for effective human oversight during use.
The answer does not mention that human oversight aims to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights.
The answer refers to oversight measures being either built in by the provider or implemented by the deployer, as per Article 14(3).
The answer does not state that overseers must be enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system as specified in Article 14(4).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.
criteria_text: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
criterion_remarks: The answer affirms the existence of exceptions in Article 53(2).
The answer states the model must be released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution.
The answer specifies that parameters, including weights, architecture, and usage information, must be made publicly available.
The answer clearly limits the exception to points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), and explicitly states that (c) and (d) still apply.
The answer states the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, which remain subject to full obligations.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a coherent, regulatory-appropriate manner without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices in Article 5 attracts the highest tier of administrative fine under the Regulation: up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). That ceiling covers breach of any of the eight prohibitions in Article 5(1), manipulative or deceptive techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or social or economic situation, social scoring, criminal-risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits, untargeted scraping of facial images, emotion inference in the workplace or education, biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Where the offender is an SME, including a start-up, the applicable ceiling is the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount (Article 99(6)). The fine must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive and set with regard to the gravity and nature of the infringement (Article 99(1) and (7)). This tier sits above the EUR 15 000 000 / 3 % tier of Article 99(4) and the EUR 7 500 000 / 1 % tier of Article 99(5).
criteria_text: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the fine amount and the turnover percentage, specifying that the higher of the two applies, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer explicitly links the fine to non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices in Article 5, satisfying the second criterion by stating the applicable scope.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality; well-organized prose suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;
criteria_text: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person
criterion_remarks: The answer states that deep fakes are AI-generated or manipulated content, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies image, audio or video content, which matches the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the content resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response is in neutral, professional language, directly quoting the definition from the Act in a clear and concise manner suitable for a regulatory context.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
criteria_text: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies high-risk systems under Article 6 and references both Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases), capturing the full substance of the criterion.
The answer states that limited-risk systems carry transparency duties under Article 50, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer notes that minimal-risk systems avoid high-risk obligations and mentions voluntary codes of conduct under Article 95, thereby stating the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose suitable for regulatory advice; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).
criteria_text: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, clearly affirming the possibility.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(a) by explaining that putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market results in being considered a provider.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(b) by describing substantial modification of a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk as a triggering condition.

The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(c) by explaining that modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk results in provider status.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Article 1 sets out the Regulation's subject matter: its purpose is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation (Article 1(1)).
criteria_text: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of improving the functioning of the internal market as a purpose of the Regulation.
The answer explicitly mentions promoting the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI.
The answer includes the full scope of protection—health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection—against harmful effects of AI systems.
The answer concludes by stating that the Regulation supports innovation, matching the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear, grammatically complete prose that directly conveys regulatory content without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).
criteria_text: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as the initial verdict, which matches the required 'No' in criterion 1 and is unambiguous.

The answer explicitly states that structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task and cites the correct provision, Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a), satisfying the substance of the criterion.

The answer clearly excludes profiling of natural persons from the derogation by stating 'the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons', which captures the exception in the criterion.
The answer references Article 6(4) and states the provider must document the assessment before market placement or putting into service, which matches the requirement in the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; well-structured and coherent prose suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Under Article 101(5) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Commission fixing a fine under that Article, and it may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed. This is a full-merits review rather than mere annulment review: the Court may substitute its own assessment of the amount for the Commission's, including raising the fine above the level the Commission set, subject to the ceiling in Article 101(1) of 3 % of the provider's annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher. The Court's review extends to whether the fine respects the criteria the Commission must apply, the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, proportionality and appropriateness under Article 101(1), and the requirement in Article 101(3) that fines be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.
criteria_text: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the Court has 'unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Commission fixing a fine', which conveys the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states the Court may 'cancel the fine', satisfying criterion 2.
The answer explicitly states the Court may 'reduce the fine', satisfying criterion 3.
The answer explicitly states the Court may 'increase the fine', satisfying criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear, coherent structure and no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: A provider (or its authorised representative) registering a high-risk Annex III system must enter the Section A data of Annex VIII into the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service (Article 49(1); Article 71(2)). Those items are: the provider's name, address and contact details; where another person submits on the provider's behalf, that person's name, address and contact details; the authorised representative's name, address and contact details, where applicable; the AI system's trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing its identification and traceability; a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported through the system; a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic; the system's status (on the market, in service, no longer placed on the market or in service, recalled); the type, number and expiry date of the notified body's certificate and that body's name or identification number; a scanned copy of that certificate, where applicable; the Member States in which the system is or has been placed on the market, put into service or made available; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; electronic instructions for use, which are not provided for systems in law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management under Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7; and, optionally, a URL for additional information.
criteria_text: Contact details of the provider, of any person submitting on its behalf and of the authorised representative, where applicable (Annex VIII, Section A, points 1 to 3)
AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (point 4)
Intended purpose and the components and functions the system supports (point 5)
Basic and concise description of the data and inputs used and the operating logic (point 6)
Market status and the notified body certificate details with a scanned copy, where applicable (points 7 to 9)
Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use (points 10 to 12)
criterion_remarks: The answer includes the provider's contact details, those of any person submitting on its behalf, and the authorised representative where applicable.
The answer states the requirement for the AI system's trade name and an unambiguous reference for identification and traceability.
The answer specifies a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported by the system.
The answer includes a basic and concise description of the data, inputs, and operating logic.
The answer covers the system's status and the notified body certificate details including type, number, expiry date, body identification, and scanned copy where applicable.
The answer lists the Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity, and electronic instructions for use, noting the exception for certain systems.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and complete sentences, suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.
criteria_text: Language: drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established
Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)
criterion_remarks: The answer states the certificate must be drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies that the validity period may not exceed five years for Annex I systems and four years for Annex III systems, conveying the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive
criterion_remarks: Answer states processing is allowed only when strictly necessary and cannot be effectively fulfilled with other data, including synthetic or anonymised.
Answer includes technical limitations on re-use and specifies state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation.
Answer covers strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations and prohibits transmission or access by others.
Answer explicitly states deletion upon bias correction or end of retention period, whichever comes first.
Answer notes that records must document the necessity and why other data types would not suffice.
Answer clarifies that the conditions are in addition to, not a substitute for, GDPR, EUDPR, and the Law Enforcement Directive.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in clear, coherent prose suitable for regulatory use.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Under Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the provider must accompany a high-risk AI system with instructions for use in an appropriate digital or other format, containing at least six categories of information. First, the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, of its authorised representative. Second, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, comprising the intended purpose; the level of accuracy including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity under Article 15 against which the system was tested and validated, and circumstances affecting that expected level; known or foreseeable circumstances of intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse that may pose risks to health, safety or fundamental rights under Article 9(2); where applicable, technical capabilities to explain output; where appropriate, performance regarding specific persons or groups; where appropriate, input-data specifications and information on the training, validation and testing datasets; and, where applicable, information enabling deployers to interpret and appropriately use the output. Third, changes to the system and its performance pre-determined by the provider at the initial conformity assessment, if any. Fourth, the human oversight measures under Article 14, including technical measures facilitating deployers' interpretation of outputs. Fifth, the computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime, and any necessary maintenance and care measures with their frequency, including software updates. Sixth, where relevant, a description of the mechanisms allowing deployers to properly collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12.
criteria_text: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity and contact details.

The answer comprehensively covers all sub-elements of characteristics, capabilities, and performance limitations, including intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity, foreseeable risks, explainability, performance for specific groups, and input data specifications.
The answer clearly includes pre-determined changes to the system and its performance as required.
The answer explicitly references human oversight measures under Article 14, including technical measures to facilitate interpretation of outputs.
The answer includes computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime, and maintenance measures with frequency, including software updates.
The answer includes, where relevant, a description of logging mechanisms in accordance with Article 12.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; directly responsive and actionable.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, while the AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate their drawing up. Article 95(3) adds that they may be developed with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society organisations and academia, and may cover one or more AI systems taking into account the similarity of the intended purpose of the relevant systems. Article 95(1) obliges the AI Office and the Member States to encourage and facilitate codes, including related governance mechanisms, fostering voluntary application to AI systems other than high-risk ones of some or all of the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. Article 95(2) requires those same bodies to facilitate codes on voluntary application, including by deployers, of specific requirements to all AI systems, on the basis of clear objectives and key performance indicators. Article 95(4) requires them to take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, when doing so. Annex VII, point 4(a)-(c) concerns notified-body applications and supplies nothing on codes of conduct.
criteria_text: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct
criterion_remarks: The answer states that codes may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers, by organisations representing them, or by both, which captures the substance of criterion 1.

The answer explicitly mentions involvement of interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia, as permitted under Article 95(3), satisfying criterion 2.
The answer clearly states that the AI Office and Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, citing Article 95(1) and (2), satisfying criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; well-structured and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1), a provider's quality management system must ensure compliance with the Regulation and be documented in a systematic and orderly manner in written policies, procedures and instructions, including at least the following aspects: (a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, covering conformity assessment procedures and the management of modifications to the system; (b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for design, design control and design verification; (c) the same for development, quality control and quality assurance; (d) examination, test and validation procedures before, during and after development, and their frequency; (e) technical specifications, including standards, and the means used where harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all Section 2 requirements; (f) systems and procedures for data management (acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention); (g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9; (h) the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72; (i) procedures for reporting serious incidents under Article 73; (j) handling of communication with national competent and other authorities, notified bodies, operators, customers and other interested parties; (k) systems and procedures for record-keeping; (l) resource management, including security-of-supply measures; (m) an accountability framework setting out management and staff responsibilities. Implementation is proportionate to the provider's organisational size (Article 17(2)).
criteria_text: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly includes a strategy for regulatory compliance covering conformity assessment and modification management.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Under Article 5(1)(h), the prohibition on 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes does not apply where such use is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives. Article 5(1)(h)(i) permits the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons. Article 5(1)(h)(ii) permits the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack. Article 5(1)(h)(iii) permits the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation or prosecution or executing a criminal penalty, for offences referred to in Annex II punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years. Use is confined to confirming the identity of a specifically targeted individual and requires a completed fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registration of the system under Article 49, which for Annex III point 1 systems is made in a secure non-public section of the EU database containing only the information specified in Article 49(4)(a), (d).
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the permitted objective of targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons as listed in Article 5(1)(h)(i).
The answer includes the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine terrorist threat, as permitted under Article 5(1)(h)(ii).

The answer correctly identifies the localisation or identification of a suspect for serious offences listed in Annex II punishable by at least four years' imprisonment, as required under Article 5(1)(h)(iii).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)). Those technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of content types, implementation costs and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as reflected in relevant technical standards. The duty does not apply where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (Article 50(2)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the Chapter V obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, and it entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office (Article 88(1)). Those powers are exercised taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94, and the delegation to the AI Office operates without prejudice to the Commission's own powers of organisation and to the division of competences between the Member States and the Union based on the Treaties (Article 88(1)). National market surveillance authorities have no enforcement competence over Chapter V; without prejudice to Article 75(3), they may only request the Commission to exercise those powers where necessary and proportionate to assist with their own tasks (Article 88(2)). Correspondingly, GPAI providers must cooperate as necessary with the Commission and the national competent authorities in the exercise of their competences and powers (Article 53(3)). The other statutory limbs flagged for this ask have no bearing on the allocation of enforcement competence and are not addressed.

AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Data collected and processed for the purpose of testing high-risk AI systems in real world conditions may be transferred to third countries only provided that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented (Article 60(4)(e)). This is a cumulative condition: it applies alongside the other conditions in Article 60(4) that must all be met for the testing itself to be lawful, and it does not displace them. In practice the "safeguards under Union law" are those of Union data protection law, the Chapter V transfer mechanisms of the GDPR (adequacy decision, appropriate safeguards, or a derogation), reinforced where the testing involves special categories of personal data. Testing data remains subject to the informed-consent and deletion requirements attached to test subjects (Article 60(4)(i)). The evidence supplies no further transfer-specific limbs beyond Article 60(4)(e).

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions are alternatives, not cumulative: under Article 51(1) a general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it meets any of the listed conditions. The first condition (Article 51(1)(a)) is that the model has high-impact capabilities, evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; "high-impact capabilities" means capabilities that match or exceed those recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models (Article 3(64)). The second condition (Article 51(1)(b)) is that, based on a decision of the Commission, taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, the model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those in point (a), having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII. Article 51(2) adds a rebuttable presumption rather than a further cumulative requirement: a model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities under point (a) where the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10^25. The Commission may amend these thresholds and supplement the benchmarks and indicators by delegated act (Article 51(3)).

Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. Classification under Article 6(1) requires both conditions to be met cumulatively: the AI system must be a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in satisfied here, since Regulation (EU) 2017/745 is listed in Annex I, point 11, and, under Article 6(1)(b), that product must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. A Class I device that is non-sterile, non-measuring and not a reusable surgical instrument is self-certified without notified body involvement, so point (b) fails. The system could still be high-risk under Article 6(2) if it falls within a listed Annex III use case.

Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualifies as high-risk where the two cumulative conditions of Article 6(1) are met, irrespective of whether it is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift. First, under Article 6(1)(a), it must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or be itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; lifts and safety components for lifts fall under Directive 2014/33/EU, listed at Annex I, point 4. Second, under Article 6(1)(b), the lift (or the AI system as a product) must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that Directive with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service. This is the Annex I product route, so the Article 6(3) derogation, which is confined to Annex III systems, cannot disapply it. Conformity assessment then follows Article 43(3): the procedure required by Directive 2014/33/EU, with the Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment.

Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Both duties apply cumulatively and immediately; neither is deferred to the market surveillance authority. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring it into conformity, withdraw, disable or recall it as appropriate, and inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. Under Article 20(2), where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the certificate under Article 44, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. The authority's own evaluation under Article 79(2) is additional: operators must cooperate as necessary and comply with any required corrective action within the period prescribed, and Article 79(4) obliges the operator to ensure corrective action across all systems concerned made available on the Union market.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: Repurposing a toy drone does not change the test: classification still turns on Article 6(1). The AI is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or itself is, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in for toys, Directive 2009/48/EC (Annex I, point 2), and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment. If the altered use takes it outside the toy directive's scope, whichever other Annex I act covers it governs instead.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply proceed on the strength of that advice, and yes, the operator must keep the logs. Using the system for a purpose outside the one specified by the provider breaches the operator's deployer duty under Article 26(1) to use it in accordance with the instructions for use, whose content (including the intended purpose) is fixed by Article 13(3)(b)(i). More seriously, Article 25(1) provides that a deployer who modifies the intended purpose of a high-risk AI system, or makes a substantial modification to it, is considered a provider of that system and assumes the full provider obligations, with the original provider owing you cooperation and technical access under Article 25(2). The operator's legal team's conclusion that neither Annex I's twenty listed Union harmonisation acts nor Annex III's eight areas covers the new use does not declassify the deployed system. Classification is governed by Article 6, and the "no significant risk" derogation in Article 6(3) is a documented provider self-assessment available only to Annex III systems. On logs, Article 26(6) requires the operator to retain the logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent under the operator's control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and in any event at least six months, unless Union or national law, particularly data protection law, provides otherwise. The evidence supplied contains no text for Article 10(2), Article 12(2) or Article 43(1), so I cannot state those limbs here.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes. Clinical decision-support software recommending best treatment is potentially high-risk, but via the product route rather than the listed-use route: under Article 6(1) it is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and requires third-party conformity assessment, here Annex I, point 11 (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices), with in vitro diagnostic software falling under Annex I, point 12.

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.

Under Article 53(1)(b) and Annex XII.1, the information given to downstream providers must include the date of release and methods of distribution (point (c)), how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software not part of it, where applicable (point (d)), the architecture and number of parameters (point (f)), and the licence (point (h)). rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, "healthcare decision making" is not itself one of the Annex III areas; clinical decision support is only caught where it falls within a specific listed use case or under the Annex I product route. Annex III lists eight areas of high-risk use cases: biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes. Only a lettered use case under one of these headings makes a system high-risk under Article 6(2). Health-related entries sit inside area 5: Annex III(5)(a) covers systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them; Annex III(5)(c) covers risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance; Annex III(5)(d) covers triage and dispatch of emergency first response, including emergency healthcare patient triage. Separately, under Article 6(1) an AI system that is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device or in vitro diagnostic device requiring third-party conformity assessment is high-risk.

No

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Guardrails alone cannot move an AI system out of the high-risk class: classification under Article 6 turns on the Annex I product route or on falling within an Annex III listed use-case, not on the strength of mitigation, and Article 8(1) makes clear that the Article 9 risk-management system is how a high-risk system achieves compliance with Section 2, not how it escapes classification, the Regulation has no "moderate risk" tier. Guardrails are instead documented as risk-management and validation measures in the Annex IV technical documentation (general description, design specifications, system architecture, computational resources, human-oversight and risk-control measures) and disclosed to deployers under Article 13(3)(b): intended purpose (i); tested accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels (ii); known or foreseeable circumstances, including reasonably foreseeable misuse, leading to Article 9(2) risks (iii); capabilities to explain output (iv); performance on specific persons or groups (v); input-data and training/validation/testing specifications (vi); and information enabling deployers to interpret output (vii), supported by Article 12(2) logging of start/stop, input reference data and post-market-relevant events. Changing capabilities and intended purpose can change classification, since the intended purpose determines whether the system falls under an Annex III use-case at all and whether the Article 6(3) derogation applies (narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or a preparatory task, never available where the system profiles natural persons), with the self-assessment documented before placing on the market. Note the converse under Article 25(1): a party that makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose so the system becomes high-risk, assumes full provider obligations.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, such use is permitted: generating illustrative images of skin conditions is not among the practices prohibited by Article 5, and teaching use does not itself make the system high-risk. Disclosure is nonetheless required: under Article 50(4) a university deploying an AI system that generates or manipulates image content constituting a deep fake, AI-generated content resembling existing persons and falsely appearing authentic (Article 3(60)), must disclose that the content is artificially generated or manipulated. The lighter regime does not apply: Article 50(4) limits transparency to non-intrusive disclosure only where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work, and exempts only use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; educational illustration is neither. Providers must additionally mark outputs machine-readably under Article 50(2).
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that generating illustrative images for teaching is not prohibited, hence permitted.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4) for deep fake content generated by AI systems.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No. Opting out of third-party conformity assessment does not disapply Chapter III, Section 2. Under Article 6(1), an AI system that is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and required to undergo third-party conformity assessment is high-risk, and Article 43(3) provides that the Section 2 requirements apply to such systems and form part of the sectoral assessment. Its final subparagraph is decisive: where a legal act listed in Section A of Annex I enables the manufacturer to opt out of third-party conformity assessment on condition that all harmonised standards covering the relevant requirements have been applied, the manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all requirements set out in Section 2. The opt-out is therefore conditioned on Section 2 compliance, not an exemption from it, and using it without that coverage makes the opt-out itself unlawful. Article 43(1)(a), (d) concerns only Annex III point 1 systems and does not apply. The supplied evidence contains no text for Article 41(1)(a)(i), (iv).
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones

The answer states that Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment, citing Article 43(3) and explaining the integration.
